title: 4-directional neighbor iteration
description: The dirs-array idiom for iterating a cell's 4 orthogonal neighbors with a bounds check — the scaffold every grid DFS/BFS starts from.

notes: Row first, column second — [dr, dc]. Mixing up the order is the #1 grid bug.
[-1, 0] is UP (row decreases), [1, 0] is DOWN — y-axis is flipped vs. math graphs.
Bounds check BEFORE indexing grid[nr][nc] — JS won't throw, it returns undefined and silently breaks comparisons.
Derive rows/cols once; grid[0].length assumes a rectangular grid (always true in interview problems).

questions.q: In `const dirs = [[-1,0],[1,0],[0,-1],[0,1]]`, which entry moves UP one row?
questions.explain: Row decreases as you move up the grid, so dr = -1.

questions.q: Would `[1, 1]` (down + right) be visited by the standard 4-directional dirs array?
options: No, that's a diagonal — 4-directional only covers up/down/left/right
Only if the grid is square
questions.explain: 4-directional means orthogonal (cardinal) neighbors only. Diagonals require the 8-way variant.

questions.q: How are `rows` and `cols` standardly derived from a 2D `grid`?
questions.explain: JS arrays expose .length, and grid[0].length is the width of the first row.

questions.q: Why must the bounds check happen BEFORE indexing `grid[nr][nc]`?
options: Style only — JS throws on out-of-bounds anyway
JS returns undefined for out-of-bounds, which silently breaks comparisons and recursion
questions.explain: Unlike many languages, JS doesn't throw on array[oob] — it quietly returns undefined, leading to subtle bugs.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the dirs array (up, down, left, right) and the bounds check for a 4-directional neighbor walk.
Use the dirs/bounds scaffold to count how many cells in the grid have at least one orthogonal neighbor equal to 0.

blanks.hint: column delta from the dirs pair

L3.prompt: Write `neighborSum(grid, r, c)` that returns the sum of the 4 orthogonal neighbors of (r, c). Treat out-of-bounds neighbors as 0. Log `neighborSum([[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]], 0, 0)` — only [1,0] (= 4) and [0,1] (= 2) are in-bounds, so the sum is 6.
hints: Derive rows = grid.length, cols = grid[0].length first.
for (const [dr, dc] of dirs) — bounds check, then add grid[nr][nc] to a running sum.
